To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effects of terminal-link stimuli on preference in concurrent-chains schedules of reinforcement depend on both the nature of the stimuli and their spatial location.

(1) pigeons prefer the shorter of two terminal links in concurrent chains with nondifferential keylight terminal-link stimuli, and (2) pigeons prefer shorter terminal links when terminal-link stimuli are differential keylights and houselights.

(a) pigeons prefer the shorter terminal-link stimulus arrangement, but (b) this preference is influenced by the stimulus arrangement of the initial link, by the stimulus location of the terminal-link stimuli, and (c) by the stimulus arrangement in the terminal-link stimuli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of terminal-link stimuli on preference in concurrent-chains schedules.
the role of conditioned reinforcers in the control of behavior and the effects of stimulus arrangements on preference.
the effects of terminal-link stimuli in the concurrent-chains procedure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
terminal-link stimuli are conditioned reinforcers and that the location and the nature of the stimuli influence preference in concurrent chains.
the terminal-link stimuli in these experiments acted as conditioned reinforcements and the stimulus location as discriminative stimuli.

the terminal link is an effective conditioned reinforcer when the terminal link is in effect on the opposite key and the stimulus is differential, and when the terminal link stimulus is differential, but not when the terminal link location is random.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
preference is determined by a combination of conditioned reinforcer value and the discriminative stimulus function of terminal-link stimuli.

the effects of terminal-link stimuli on preference in concurrent-chain schedules are determined by their function as conditioned reinforcers and their location relative to the initial-link stimuli, as well as by the stimulus properties of the terminal links themselves.
preference in concurrent chains is a joint function of the terminal-link stimuli, the location of the terminal link, and the schedule of reinforcement in the initial link.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the location of a terminal-link schedule of reinforcement is a powerful determinant of preference in concurrent-chains schedules, and this effect is independent of terminal-link stimuli and their discriminative functions.
terminal-link stimuli function as conditioned reinforcerers, rather than as simple discriminative stimuli.
